gap: No result ChatGPT got states that the BLUETTI Elite 30 V2's advertised 'only 4.5W standby' is not what it draws with the AC outlets switched on: The Technology Man saw the battery fall from 100% to 19% in 12 hours with AC enabled and Eco mode off, which works out to about 19 W, and measured only 231 Wh usable on AC. Its '1,500W Lifting Power' is also not a surge rating, because it works by lowering the output voltage.
standout_why: I compared against the cited rivals solar-home.space, campequipmentplus.com and solutionenergy.com, plus Dealectric's current page. solutionenergy.com already explains Jackery's 4,000 cycles to 70% versus others' cycles to 80%, but only for 1 kWh-class stations. campequipmentplus.com and solar-home.space give continuous and surge watts and explain panel derating and input caps, again mostly for the big units. None of them covers the Elite 30 V2. None compares the standby figure makers print with measured AC-on idle draw, gives measured usable Wh for any 288 Wh tent-size station, or says that Lifting Power is reduced-voltage operation for resistive loads only. Dealectric's page lists the Elite 30 V2 as 600 W and 288 Wh and says it covers 'CPAP one night', with no caveat about usable AC energy.
decides: The Elite 30 V2 + 100 W stays the pick. Its 600 W continuous rating is real, and its AC usable energy (231 Wh, The Technology Man) about matches the Anker C300 (230 Wh, OutdoorGearLab), so normalising does not change the ranking. What it changes is the advice. Leaving the inverter on overnight in a tent with Eco mode off costs about 19 W, or roughly 150 Wh over 8 hours, which is more than half the battery. 'CPAP one night' only holds for about a 30 W CPAP with the AC switched off when not in use, or run from the 12 V port (244 Wh usable on DC). The kit's 100 W panel uses only half the 200 W solar input, so BLUETTI's 2.2-hour solar refill figure does not apply to this kit. The 1,500 W figure should not be listed as surge.

findings.label: Maker output claim

findings.label: Maker standby claim
findings.source_title: BLUETTI Elite 30 V2 Portable Power Station | 600W 288Wh
findings.note: The wording is 'Up to 50% less self-consumption and only 4.5W standby'. The page does not say which outputs are on when this is measured.

findings.label: Measured idle draw, AC output on (Eco mode off)
findings.source_title: The Technology Man: This $189 BLUETTI Elite 30 V2 power station is better than I expected (Gidon, 2025-12-23)
findings.note: The battery fell from 100% to 19% in 12 h. 0.81 × 288 Wh = 233 Wh over 12 h = 19.4 W, about 4.3× the 4.5 W 'standby' claim. Over an 8 h night that is about 155 Wh, or 54% of 288 Wh.

findings.label: Measured idle draw, DC output on (Eco mode off)
findings.source_title: The Technology Man: This $189 BLUETTI Elite 30 V2 power station is better than I expected (Gidon, 2025-12-23)
findings.note: The battery fell from 100% to 24% in 20 h. 0.76 × 288 = 219 Wh over 20 h = 10.9 W.

findings.label: Measured usable energy
findings.value: 231 Wh on AC (about 80%), 244 Wh on DC (about 85%)
findings.source_title: The Technology Man: This $189 BLUETTI Elite 30 V2 power station is better than I expected (Gidon, 2025-12-23)
findings.note: Constant-load discharge; the article does not give the load in watts. At about 30 W from the AC outlet, 231 Wh lasts about 7.7 h, which is borderline for one CPAP night.

findings.label: What Lifting Power actually does
findings.value: Lowers output voltage; real output stays at 600 W or less; resistive loads only
findings.source_title: The Technology Man: This $189 BLUETTI Elite 30 V2 power station is better than I expected (Gidon, 2025-12-23)
findings.note: The reviewer started a 450 W air duster with no soft start, measured above 10 A (about 2,300 W) at switch-on, and it ran with Power Lifting on. That is one load test, not a published surge rating.

findings.label: Solar input cap vs kit panel
findings.value: 200 W max solar input; the kit ships a 100 W panel
findings.source_title: BLUETTI Elite 30 V2 Portable Power Station | 600W 288Wh
findings.note: The page says 'Solar Panels: 200W Max., 2.2H'. The 2.2 h refill figure assumes the full 200 W, so the kit's 100 W panel can use at most half the input. Other specs on the same page: AC charging 380 W in 70 min, weight 4.3 kg, 'Over 3,000 cycles' with no % basis.

findings.label: Cycle-life basis and solar claims
findings.value: 4,000+ cycles to 70% capacity; 300 W rated; 292 Wh LiFePO4; 7.5 lb; to 80% in about 2.8 h with a 100 W panel or 7.5 h with a 40 W panel
findings.note: Read from Jackery's Shopify listing through storecheck.py search; the full product page returned HTTP 429. The listing showed $289, available, but its text says the 40 W panel is 'sold separately', so the bundle's contents are unclear. Dealectric's page says $379 with a 40 W panel. Jackery rates to 70% while BLUETTI and Anker figures are usually to 80%, so 4,000 here is not directly comparable to their 3,000.
